scenarios.title: Leave a lane beside the net-front player
scenarios.objective: Recognize an occupied shooting path without prescribing contested net-front play.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 holds the puck in the high slot. YOU stand in the low slot directly between F1 and the goal. D1 is off to the side. This is a non-contact spacing discussion, not a screen or rebound battle.
cues: YOU occupy the F1-to-goal centre line.
The low slot is closer to the goal than the high slot.
D1 is offset from that line.

No compulsory net-front assignment is inferred. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which navy player stands directly between F1 and the goal?

options.text: YOU
D1
F1’s passer, who is not shown

questions.explanation: YOU are on the same middle line as F1 and the goal.

questions.prompt: Which questions could clarify your net-front role?

options.text: Is F1 trying to shoot or pass?
Where can YOU provide an option without crowding F1’s route?
Does standing in the low slot guarantee a goal?

questions.explanation: The intended play and available space help define the role. Location alone does not guarantee a scoring chance.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested spacing discussion.

options.text: Notice your position in F1’s line
Choose a useful nearby role or receiving angle
Recheck as F1 changes the puck position

questions.explanation: This is a spacing example. A coach may teach a deliberate screen or tip with a separate reviewed task.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a possible support spot beside the low-slot shooting line.
questions.explanation: The example keeps YOU near the goal area while opening the original centre line. Several nearby support points may be useful.

questions.prompt: If F1 decides to pass to YOU instead of shooting, what should you check next?

options.text: The new receiving line and D1’s reach
Only whether YOU are nearest the crease
The old shooting line without the puck’s new plan

questions.explanation: A passing role needs a usable receiving line; the previous shooting discussion no longer supplies the whole answer.

questions.prompt: How could you explain “beside the shot lane” without saying “move to my dot”?
questions.explanation: Describe your relationship to F1, the goal and D1. Another point can satisfy the same relationship.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate beside F1?

options.text: I am beside the lane; show me if the pass opens
I will occupy the same lane
The goalie guarantees a rebound

questions.explanation: The message preserves F1's lane and makes the support conditional on visibility.

questions.prompt: Which two changes should move your support spot?

options.text: F1 changes from shot to pass
D1 follows toward your side
The goalie remains in the crease

questions.explanation: The carrier action and defender response change the support relationship; the goalie location alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a separate support angle beside the net-front lane.
questions.explanation: This point leaves F1 in the lane and offers a reachable side angle.

questions.prompt: D1 follows you into the side space. How can F1 still use the movement?
questions.explanation: D1’s movement may open F1’s lane or a pass from F1 to YOU. Call the new space and re-check the goalie before choosing.

scenarios.title: Defend the middle before chasing wide
scenarios.objective: Relate a carrier, a wide teammate and the defended goal when planning inside position.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are the gold defender protecting the right net. Navy F1 carries toward you; F2 is wide across the rink from the carrier. No skating speed is given. Plan where YOU might stay connected to the middle threat.
cues: YOU are between the carrier and the defended goal.
F2 is a separate wide option.
Gap depends on movement that a static distance cannot prove.

questions.prompt: Which net is YOU protecting as the gold defender?

options.text: The right net
The left net
Only the side boards beside F1

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns YOU to gold, which defends the right end while navy attacks it.

questions.prompt: What should your gap decision relate?

options.text: F1’s approach and control
The middle route toward the defended goal
Only the largest possible distance from F1

questions.explanation: Useful spacing balances pressure with the ability to protect and recover. Maximum distance is not a general solution.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested defensive read.

options.text: Locate carrier, support and defended goal
Choose an inside position you can maintain
Adjust when the carrier’s movement changes

questions.explanation: This is an original planning routine. A real gap requires speed and turning information.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example inside position between F1 and the middle.
questions.explanation: The sample remains goal-side while slightly adjusting toward the carrier. Other positions may fit different speeds or support responsibilities.

questions.prompt: If F1 accelerates and begins to get beside YOU, what should you reconsider?

options.text: How to recover while protecting the route to goal
Whether the original distance must remain fixed
Whether YOU should follow F2 regardless of the carrier

questions.explanation: A speed change can require an earlier turn or recovery. The freeze cannot choose an exact skating response.

questions.prompt: Why is there no single “correct gap number” in this picture?
questions.explanation: Explain which missing movement or control information could change the useful spacing. A distance alone is not the tactical answer.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate while holding the inside gap?

options.text: I am protecting the middle; update me if F1 reaches the outside
I will close to one exact distance
F2 is the only threat

questions.explanation: The call names the protected middle and the carrier route that would change the job.

questions.prompt: Which two cues can require a new gap read?

options.text: F1 changes speed
F1 changes the route toward the net
The rink stays the same size

questions.explanation: Carrier speed and route change the useful gap; fixed rink geometry does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an inside net-side position with F1 ahead.
questions.explanation: This point keeps a net-side relationship to F1 and leaves F2 visible.

questions.prompt: F1 gets outside your starting gap. Explain the recovery choice.
questions.explanation: Protect the net-side lane, match F1's route, and re-check F2 rather than chasing the old inside spot.

scenarios.title: Angle the carrier away from the slot
scenarios.objective: Use an inside approach to influence a wide carrier without assuming a forced turnover.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are gold and defend the right goal. F1 carries toward the half wall on the same side. F2 waits across the slot. Consider an approach that limits the route into the middle.
cues: YOU start closer to the middle than F1.
F1 is wide near the half-wall side.
F2 remains a possible cross-ice receiver.

sources.title: 7 Principles for Coaches: Angling
sources.section: Limiting Opponent Options; Anticipation & Body Positioning
sources.use: Supports steering through position; no fixed distance or guaranteed turnover.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The example is an approach-angle discussion, not contact instruction. Stick reach, skating and successful containment are unvalidated. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Compared with F1, where does YOU start across the rink width?

options.text: Closer to the middle
Closer to the side boards beside F1
Behind the right net

questions.explanation: YOU are at y=2 and F1 at y=7; the middle is around y=0.

questions.prompt: What does an inside approach try to preserve here?

options.text: Awareness of the carrier’s route into the slot
A chance to adjust if F1 changes direction
Certainty that F2 cannot receive a pass

questions.explanation: An approach can influence space while preserving adjustment. It cannot guarantee that all passing options disappear.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested angling plan.

options.text: Read F1’s direction and the inside space
Approach from an angle that protects that space
Update the approach if F1 turns or passes

questions.explanation: This is a conditional approach plan, not a promise to win possession.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward an approach that stays inside F1’s current wide route.
questions.explanation: The sample closes some wide space while staying nearer the middle and goal-side. Exact timing may require a different point.

questions.prompt: Suppose F1 turns back toward centre ice instead of driving the slot. What should YOU reassess?

options.text: The new direction before continuing pressure
The same straight chase toward the old spot
A completed turnover that has not happened

questions.explanation: The carrier changed the threat. Re-reading can preserve balance and avoid chasing the old route.

questions.prompt: How could you describe an angling route using the slot and half wall?
questions.explanation: Explain which middle route you protect and which wider space you might allow. A useful answer names the relationship, not just “pressure.”

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell F1 from the inside angle?

options.text: The middle is protected; the half-wall route is the space to read
You must skate to the wall
The route is fixed

questions.explanation: The communication describes the visible relationship and keeps F1's route conditional.

questions.prompt: Which two cues change the angle?

options.text: F1 cuts toward the middle
F2 enters the wide route
YOU sees the puck

questions.explanation: Carrier and support movements change the inside relationship; puck visibility alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU inside F1 while leaving the half-wall route visible.
questions.explanation: This point remains inside the carrier and preserves room to update.

questions.prompt: F1 turns toward the middle. What do you re-read?
questions.explanation: Match F1's new route, protect the slot, and check whether F2 changes the wide lane before choosing the next angle.

scenarios.title: Recover after the first reach misses
scenarios.objective: Recognize when a missed challenge changes the job from reaching to recovery.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are gold. Your first stick reach missed, and F1 has moved beyond you toward the right net. This is a no-contact recovery drill; F2 is a second navy attacker.
cues: The missed reach is given in the briefing.
F1 is closer to the right goal line than YOU.
F2 offers a separate attacking route.

sources.section: U11 Skills Matrix, printed page 22 (PDF page 22)

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The U11 matrix supports recovery-related skating and individual defence topics; it does not show whether YOU can catch F1. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: After the stated missed reach, which attacker has moved beyond YOU toward the right net?

options.text: F2 has the puck behind YOU.
F1 has the puck closer to the right goal line.
YOU still own the puck.

questions.explanation: F1 owns the puck at x = 15; YOU are at x = 13. The briefing also states that F1 passed the first challenge.

questions.prompt: Which details should guide your recovery route now?

options.text: F1’s route toward the net
F2’s possible receiving lane
Only where F1 stood before your missed reach

questions.explanation: Recover with the current carrier and the second attacker in view. Chasing the old location spends time on a cue that has already changed.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested recovery response after the missed reach.

options.text: Recognize that the first challenge is over.
Turn and move toward a useful defensive route.
Recheck the puck and the second attacker as you recover.

questions.explanation: This is a recovery routine, not a promise that the defender can regain position. The recheck can happen repeatedly while moving.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example recovery destination between the attack and the right net. Explain the route you would need to skate.
questions.explanation: The reference is nearer the defended net and inside the carrier’s wide route. It is a future destination, not an instant recovery or proof that this route is reachable before the attackers.

questions.prompt: Suppose F1 then slows and turns toward the side boards while F2 drives the middle. What should update your read?

options.text: Keep reaching toward F1’s old position.
Ignore F2 because F1 owns the puck.
Recheck the middle threat and whether a teammate can handle the carrier.

questions.explanation: The developing middle route may matter more than another distant reach. Team support and actual timing determine whether YOU recover toward F2 or can challenge F1 again.

questions.prompt: Why is a second reach from behind sometimes less useful than recovering toward the net?
questions.explanation: A reach that cannot affect the puck can delay recovery and leave the middle open. Explain the distance, skating direction and second attacker; a safe reachable stick play can still be useful.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call after the missed reach?

options.text: F1 is ahead; I am recovering toward the net-side lane
The puck is won already
F2 is no longer relevant

questions.explanation: The call identifies the missed reach and the new net-side priority.

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape your recovery?

options.text: F1's route to the right net
F2's wide position
The first reach must be repeated

questions.explanation: The two attackers define the recovery relationship; repeating the reach is not a decision rule.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to the net-side space between F1 and the goal.
questions.explanation: This point recovers toward the dangerous lane while keeping F2 in view.

questions.prompt: F1 slows at the boards while F2 drives middle. Explain the updated job.
questions.explanation: Protect the new middle threat while staying connected to F1. Name which attacker is more dangerous from the changed space.

scenarios.title: Backcheck the uncovered runner
scenarios.objective: Separate the carrier’s pressure from a second attacker’s route.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are gold, returning toward the right net. The coach has assigned gold D1 to the navy puck carrier F1 for this rep. Navy F2 is moving through the other side of the middle; this movement is stated rather than animated.
cues: D1 has the carrier assignment for this rep.
F2 is a separate navy runner.

questions.prompt: Who is already assigned to the carrier in this practice rep?

options.text: Gold D1
Gold YOU
Navy F2

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly assigns gold D1 to navy F1, who owns the puck. That assignment creates a separate support decision for YOU.

questions.prompt: Before choosing your backcheck route, what information belongs in the read?

options.text: Whether F2 can receive toward the middle
Whether D1 still has pressure on F1
Whether YOU can see both the runner and puck

questions.explanation: These three cues connect your responsibility to the live play. The initial assignment may need to change if D1 loses the carrier.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested backcheck check-in.

options.text: Identify who is pressuring the carrier.
Find the separate runner and choose an inside recovery route.
Keep checking for a pass or a changed assignment.

questions.explanation: The routine helps avoid two defenders following the puck while another attacker is available. It is not a command to ignore a reachable puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a useful defensive relationship with F2 and the right net. Multiple recovery spots may work.
questions.explanation: The reference places YOU nearer the right net than F2 and close to the runner’s route. This illustrates a goal-side relationship; it does not prove interception timing or prescribe a fixed gap.

questions.prompt: If D1 falls behind F1 and calls for help, how should YOU respond?

options.text: Keep the original assignment without looking again.
Recheck the immediate net threat and communicate who can cover F2.
Automatically skate to the far corner.

questions.explanation: New pressure information can change the responsibilities. Helping on the carrier may be needed, but F2’s route should remain part of the decision rather than disappearing from the read.

questions.prompt: What would make your backcheck different from simply skating toward the puck?
questions.explanation: Describe the teammate already applying pressure, the uncovered runner, and your route toward the defended net. A strong explanation also states what new cue would make you switch responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate on the backcheck?

options.text: D1 has F1; I am tracking F2 toward the right net
I am chasing the puck only
F2 does not receive

questions.explanation: The call identifies the uncovered runner and the teammate pressure.

questions.prompt: Which two events can change your backcheck?

options.text: F2 cuts toward the net
D1 loses contact with F1
The puck stays with F1

questions.explanation: The runner route and teammate pressure determine whether the backcheck job shifts.

questions.prompt: Move YOU between F2 and the right net.
questions.explanation: This point places YOU on the defended net-side of F2 and keeps F1 visible; the recovery route remains conditional on F2’s movement.

questions.prompt: D1 calls for help after falling behind F1. How do you choose?
questions.explanation: Re-scan F1 and F2, then support the more dangerous reachable lane without losing sight of the second attacker.
